justification: Abstract's object is evaluator authorization: locally validated steps failing to compose, with gluing-defect diagnostics; it proves a conditional kernel theorem and offers a calculus, no study, so a conceptual framework.

Nexus's named novelty is an adaptive selector choosing Direct vs ReAct vs Plan-and-Execute per task, i.e. what the loop does next; evaluated on 500 real enterprise tasks with production deployment lessons.
Both systems contribute interactive task decomposition into editable subgoals or phases that fix the next step; evidence is a lab within-subjects experiment (n=18) with prototypes, not deployed use.
Headline artefact is CARA, automated metrics auditing debate behaviour and naming the consistency-illusion failure mode; measured on MedQA-USMLE and MedThink-Bench in the lab.

Contribution is the arrangement itself: a pipeline of interpretation, synthesis, validation and correction agents; the paper analyses the architecture and asserts superiority without a measured study.

XPS 2's mechanism is a rule-based controller that must verify every LLM hypothesis before it can influence decisions; the paper outlines design principles and demonstrates on fault diagnosis, no measurement.

The claim concerns the arrangement of role-differentiated agents in a shared context and prescribes injecting a heterogeneous external agent; it is a conceptual account of a failure mode with no method or data.

Its distinguishing claim is an integrated monitor combining internal reasoning with execution results to detect abnormal behaviour; a prototype is run on task scenarios against existing methods in the lab.
The thesis is that coordination topology determines failure geometry, i.e. the arrangement of agents; the paper is explicitly a heuristic synthesis over seven preprints, not a derivation or a study.

TUMIX runs diverse tool-use agents in parallel and selects among their answer paths, changing the shape of candidate exploration; gains reported on standard reasoning benchmarks with Gemini backbones.
SI-Agent's outer loop rewrites the agent's own system instructions from reward feedback across cycles; experiments compare it to baselines on task performance and readability in the lab.
The contribution is the revision law: treating output deviation as an error term driving iterative prompt refinement; only a control-theoretic mathematical foundation is offered, with no evaluation.
Agent-R trains the model on self-constructed revision trajectories, an outer loop changing the agent between episodes; effectiveness shown by experiments in interactive agent environments.

Retroformer learns a retrospective model by policy gradient that rewrites the agent's prompt from environment rewards across episodes; validated experimentally on agent tasks against non-gradient baselines.
MOSAIC structures inference as plan, check, then act or refuse, a safety gate on each action; evaluated zero-shot on out-of-distribution harmful-task, injection and privacy benchmarks.
The reward designs suppress excessive tool calls, cutting calls by 72% to control cost and latency; evidence is pilot entropy experiments plus benchmark runs across domains against baselines.

The framework closes injection, diagnosis and refinement: a rule-based diagnoser's structured labels drive an optimizer that rewrites payloads; measured on AgentDojo and InjectAgent against baselines.
The question is whether revising hypotheses on experimental feedback helps at all; 800 replicated runs with a permuted-feedback control condition and p-values make it a lab experiment.
The artefact is a 180-task ABAP measurement suite used to instrument how models exploit compiler feedback over iterations; results are lab benchmark success rates across models.
ToolBench-X is an instrument: executable tasks with five injected hazard types and recovery paths for measuring agent loops; the paper reports benchmark results for agents in the lab.
MINT is a benchmark plus evaluation harness for multi-turn tool use and language feedback; twenty models are measured on it in the lab, with user feedback simulated inside each turn.
DGM iteratively rewrites its own code and keeps validated variants, an outer loop that changes the agent itself; each self-modification is empirically checked on coding benchmarks.
The distinctive mechanism is a memory optimization based on the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve governing what carries across long-span tasks; the abstract argues the design and reports no measurement.
CER accumulates past trajectories in a dynamic memory buffer and retrieves them into the context window, a training-free state-carrying mechanism; evaluated on WebArena and VisualWebArena.
ERL stores reflected heuristics and selectively retrieves them into context, and its ablation credits retrieval; success-rate gains are measured on the Gaia2 benchmark against a ReAct baseline.
